1. Core Clinical Tension: A 61-year-old woman presents with subacute malaise, bibasilar lung rales, and large pericardial and pleural effusions. Initial diagnostic workup including pericardial fluid cytology, acid-fast smears, T-SPOT, Xpert MTB/RIF, and tumor markers was non-diagnostic, initially suggesting non-specific idiopathic or neoplastic exudative pericarditis before recurring 2 months later and demonstrating granulomatous inflammation on pericardial and mediastinal node biopsy.
2. Admission Breakpoint: Admission triage terminates after admission vitals, cardiovascular and pulmonary physical exam, ECG showing limb lead low voltage, echocardiography documenting moderate-to-severe pericardial effusion, bedside ultrasound showing pleural effusions, and chest CT demonstrating inflammatory nodules, calcification, and adenopathy, prior to pericardiocentesis, blood cultures, empirical antibiotics, PET/CT, or surgical biopsy.
3. Differential Distinctions: Community-acquired pneumonia with parapneumonic pericarditis was considered due to fever, crackles, and parenchymal nodules, but blood cultures were sterile and symptoms recurred. Malignant pericardial effusion was strongly suspected due to large exudative effusion and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, but excluded by negative fluid cytology, normal tumor markers, and PET/CT. Autoimmune serositis and hypothyroidism were excluded by negative autoimmune panel and preserved thyroid function. Tuberculous pericarditis was confirmed on pericardial and nodal histology.
case_prompt:
A 61-year-old woman presents with a 20-day history of progressive weakness and loss of appetite. Her past medical history includes cholecystitis treated by cholecystectomy several years prior.

On physical examination, her body temperature is 36.7 °C, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, and heart rate 77 beats per minute. Auscultation reveals coarse breath sounds throughout both lungs with diminished breath sounds at both bases and scattered bibasilar wet crackles. Cardiac examination reveals diminished, distant heart sounds with enlarged cardiac dullness on percussion.

Electrocardiogram demonstrates sinus rhythm with low voltage throughout the limb leads.

Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrates moderate to severe pericardial effusion with circumferential echo-free space measuring 14 mm along the right ventricular anterior wall, 16 mm posterior to the left ventricle, 19 mm lateral to the left ventricle, and 20 mm at the apex. Bedside color Doppler ultrasound shows bilateral pleural effusions.

Computed tomography (CT) of the chest reveals sporadic inflammation in both lungs, inflammatory nodules in the left upper and right lower lobes, a calcified nodule in the left upper lobe, bilateral pleural effusions, and enlarged, partially calcified mediastinal lymph nodes.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered because the patient developed intermittent fevers up to 38.3 °C with coarse pulmonary rales and inflammatory nodules on chest CT, but excluded when blood cultures showed no bacterial growth and symptoms recurred after broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The patient's temperature was elevated within 24 h of admission, meaning that the possibility of community-acquired pneumonia could not be excluded. After blood cultures were retained, the patient was also given empirical anti-infective treatment with moxifloxacin... The patient's blood culture later indicated no bacterial growth.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Evaluated as a primary cause of massive hemorrhagic/exudative pericardial effusion and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, but excluded by negative exfoliated cytology, normal serum tumor markers, and lack of neoplastic uptake on PET/CT.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The exfoliated cells of the pericardial effusion showed lymphocytes and lobulated nuclei, and no cancer cells were found. Female tumor markers such as CEA, cancer antigen (CA) 125, CA 199, and neuron-specific enolase were below the reference values to exclude tumor-derived pericardial effusion. Further positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) was performed, which showed inhomogeneous thickening of the pericardium, enhanced metabolism, mediastinal lymph nodes, and uterine metabolism fibroids. Therefore, we could almost exclude the possibility that pericardial effusion was caused by a tumor.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered as potential etiologies of unexplained pericardial fluid accumulation, but ruled out by negative rheumatologic antibodies and minimally altered free T3.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The patient's thyroid function test suggested that her free triiodothyronine (FT3) of 2.31 pmol/L was only mildly depressed, and it was unlikely that the pericardial effusion was caused by hypothyroidism. To rule out the possibility that the patient's pericardial effusion was caused by autoimmune disease, we further performed autoimmune marker screening, and the patient's antinuclear antibodies (ANA), anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), and antiphospholipid. The antiphospholipid syndrome antibodies were all negative, which essentially excluded autoimmune diseases.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Following recurrent effusion and chest pain 2 months later, thoracic surgical biopsy of the pericardial mass and mediastinal lymph nodes revealed classic granulomatous lesions and fibrous hyperplasia, establishing tuberculous pericarditis in conjunction with lymphocyte-predominant exudate and elevated ADA.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Pathological findings showed granulomatous lesions and fibrous hyperplasia of the mediastinal lymph nodes (Figure 4) and granulomatous lesions of the pericardial fibrofatty tissue (Figure 5). Furthermore, the patient's pulmonary CT indicated a nodular calcified shadow in the left upper lung and enlarged and partially calcified lymph nodes in the mediastinum and part of the bilateral hilum. The patient was considered to have stable tuberculosis in the upper lobe of the left lung, and the pericardial puncture fluid was exudate with increased leukocytes, mainly monocytes, and mildly elevated ADA. TBP can be suspected according to the diagnostic criteria

editor_comments: Stanford MedCaseReasoning distillation. Admission prompt is strictly Day-1 triage presentation (exam, ECG, echo, triage CT). Pericardiocentesis results, send-outs, and biopsies belong exclusively to diagnostic reasoning. All quotes verified.
